title: The stick in the baby's throat
hookLine: he says what is true and helpful even when unwelcome, at the right time, as you'd pull a stick from a baby's throat (MN 58)

cards: A prince named Abhaya comes to the Buddha with a trick question someone has coached him to ask. It's built with two prongs, so that either answer sticks in the throat.
Would you ever say something that others find unwelcome and disagreeable? If the Buddha says yes, how is he different from anyone else who hurts people's feelings?
If he says no, what about the hard things he has said about the monk Devadatta? Abhaya sits down with his baby son on his lap. That small detail turns out to be the whole answer.

teach.b: The Buddha doesn't say yes or no. He looks at the baby. Prince, he asks, if this child, through someone's carelessness, put a stick or a pebble in his mouth, what would you do?
Abhaya answers at once. I'd get it out.

teach.h: I'D GET IT OUT, EVEN WITH BLOOD.
teach.b: If I couldn't get it out right away, I'd hold his head with my left hand, crook a finger of my right, and pull it out, even if it drew blood. Why? Because I have compassion for the child.

That, the Buddha says, is how he speaks. Then he lays out the cases, six of them, like a grid. If something is untrue, or true but of no help, he doesn't say it, whether people would welcome it or not.
If it's true and helpful but unwelcome, he knows the right time to say it.
If it's true, helpful and welcome, again, he knows the right time. Look at what does the deciding. Whether people will like it is on the grid, but it never settles anything.
Wounding them isn't on it at all. The deciding questions are: is it true, does it help? And then: when?

Pulling a stick from a child's throat isn't gentle in the moment. There may be crying, even a little blood. But nobody watching would call it cruel, because everyone can see what it's for and who it's for.
The sutta ends with Abhaya, who came to trap the Buddha, going for refuge instead. Some sticks come out easily.

how: Buddhist teachers often tell this story when explaining right speech, and monastic communities have a formal way of pointing out a fellow monastic's fault, raised respectfully and at a suitable time.

o: fate: what was always going to happen
time: knowing the right moment to speak
a season of rest from all speaking

whether it's welcome never decides: only true, helpful, and when.
Abhaya came to the Buddha as a devoted follower

games.q: you're Prince Abhaya. your baby son has a pebble in his mouth, and it won't come out easily. what do you do?
o: leave it; he'll cry if you interfere.
get it out, even if it draws blood.
wait for the nurse to notice.
games.why: Abhaya says he'd hold the child's head and hook it out with a finger, even drawing blood, out of compassion. the Buddha says that's how he speaks unwelcome truths.

practice: Think of one true thing someone in your life may need to hear, about their health, their work, a habit that's hurting them, and ask the Buddha's questions: is it true, will it help them, and then the hardest one, when?
Picture a moment that would be right, when they can hear it, not when you're angry or tired, and picture your hand steady and careful, the way you'd reach for a child. Rest there with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Kala, time. The Buddha's picture for a truth that's unwelcome but needed: said for the other's sake, at the right time.

orig.note: Pali kāla: time. MN 58 says the Buddha knows the right time for a hard word.

carryVoice: Your line: the right time. A needed truth waits for a moment they can hear it, and if that moment isn't today, waiting counts too. Go gently.
